questions.question: ShopFlow lands raw data in the lakehouse first and transforms it there afterwards, in layers. Which approach is this? (one answer)

options.text: ETL — transform on a separate engine, then load
ELT — load the raw data first, then transform it in place
CDC — read the database's change log
OLTP — process many small transactions

questions.explanation: **ELT** loads the raw data first and transforms it with the lakehouse's own compute, so a raw copy is always kept. Bronze *is* the loaded raw zone; Silver and Gold are the transform steps.

questions.question: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.

slots.label: An OLTP database is usually normalized: many small linked tables.
OLAP systems are usually row-oriented, to scan one column over millions of rows fast.
Running heavy reports on the production database can slow down the live app for customers.

questions.explanation: OLTP runs the business: normalized and row-oriented. OLAP understands it: denormalized and **column**-oriented. Big analytical scans on the live database compete with customers' transactions, which is why analytics runs on a separate system.

questions.question: Which **three** layers make up a lakehouse? (Choose three.)

options.text: Object storage (Parquet files on S3 / RustFS)
An open table format (Delta or Iceberg)
A catalog (e.g. Apache Polaris)
A proprietary storage engine that couples storage and compute
A separate data warehouse holding a copy of the Gold tables

questions.explanation: A lakehouse = **object storage** + an **open table format** + a **catalog**. Storage and compute stay separate, and Bronze and Gold live in the same place: no separate warehouse copy.

questions.question:
Match each storage system to how it applies a schema.

| System | Schema |
|---|---|
| Data warehouse | [Warehouse] |
| Data lake (plain files) | [Lake] |
questions.explanation: A warehouse needs data to fit a fixed schema **before** loading (schema-on-write). A lake stores files of any shape and applies structure only **when you query** (schema-on-read).

questions.question: A query on a Parquet table with 50 columns uses only 2 of them, and the engine physically reads only those 2. What is this called? (one answer)

options.text: Predicate pushdown
Projection pushdown
Partitioning
Compaction (OPTIMIZE)

questions.explanation: **Projection pushdown** reads only the columns a query needs, possible because Parquet is columnar. **Predicate pushdown** is different: it skips row groups whose min/max stats can't match a filter.

questions.question: A folder of Parquet files becomes a Delta or Iceberg table. Which **two** abilities does the table format add that plain Parquet files lack? (Choose two.)

options.text: Columnar storage
ACID transactions: a write fully happens or not at all
Compression of similar values
Time travel: query the table as it was at an earlier version
Min/max statistics per row group

questions.explanation: The table format's **transaction log** adds ACID, MERGE / update / delete, **time travel** and schema evolution. Columnar layout, compression and row-group statistics are Parquet's own features.

questions.question:
Match each description to its medallion layer.

| Description | Layer |
|---|---|
| An exact, append-only copy of the sources: keep everything | [Raw copy] |
| Cleaned, deduplicated, conformed: the single source of truth | [Clean model] |
| Aggregated marts that answer business questions directly | [Business marts] |
questions.explanation: **Bronze** keeps the raw data as it arrived, **Silver** makes it clean and conformed, **Gold** shapes it for BI and ML.

questions.question: Months after go-live you find a bug in the Silver transform. How do you fix Silver and Gold **without** fetching the data from the sources again? (one answer)

options.text: Restore yesterday's Gold backup
Rebuild Silver and Gold from the raw Bronze tables with the fixed logic
Ask the source teams to resend six months of data
Patch the Gold numbers by hand

questions.explanation: That is why Bronze keeps **everything**, even bad or duplicate rows: it is the replay buffer. Fix the logic and rebuild Silver and Gold from Bronze; no re-ingest is needed.

questions.question: The fact table has `profit` and `revenue` per order line, and a `margin_pct` column. What is the correct margin for a whole month? (one answer)

options.text: `avg(margin_pct)`
`sum(margin_pct)`
`sum(profit) / sum(revenue)`
`max(margin_pct)`

questions.explanation: A percentage is **non-additive**: never sum or average it. Keep its parts as additive measures and divide **at query time**: `sum(profit) / sum(revenue)`.

questions.question: An order line in `fact_sales` refers to a `product_sk` that has no row in `dim_product`. The report joins them with an `INNER JOIN`. What happens? (one answer)

options.text: The query fails with a foreign-key error
The line's revenue lands in a "(null)" category
The line is silently dropped, so product totals come out too low
Trino adds the missing product automatically

questions.explanation: An `INNER JOIN` silently drops the orphaned line, so its revenue vanishes and **nothing errors**. Point unknown keys at an **"Unknown" member** (e.g. `-1`) instead, and run an orphan check that should return 0.
